Supporting research: Rutter et al.'s English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) longitudinal study - children adopted before 6 months mostly caught up cognitively and in attachment, but those adopted later showed persistent disinhibited attachment and cognitive impairment, suggesting a sensitive period; Chugani et al. (1998) PET scans of Romanian adoptees showed reduced brain activity in areas linked to emotional processing; Tizard - ex-institutional children showed indiscriminate attachment to caregivers and strangers.","acceptableAlternatives":["Any accurate institutionalisation effects: disinhibited/institutional autism, developmental delay (physical/cognitive/language), attachment disorder, later parenting difficulties","Any valid Romanian orphanage research: Rutter ERA study, Chugani PET scan study, Tizard adoption study, Zeanah Bucharest Early Intervention Project","Effects may be presented as general consequences of institutional care or specifically tied to Romanian orphanage findings; theory described in detail and accurately; evaluation is effective, well-balanced between supporting and challenging evidence, and explicitly linked back to the theory; conclusions drawn about the status of the theory."}],"traits":[{"trait":"AO1 - Knowledge and description of Bowlby's theory of maternal deprivation","maxMarks":6,"bands":[{"min":0,"max":0,"code":"0","descriptor":"No relevant knowledge."},{"min":1,"max":2,"code":"1","descriptor":"Fragmentary or inaccurate description of the theory."},{"min":3,"max":4,"code":"2","descriptor":"Reasonable description of key elements of the theory with some detail."},{"min":5,"max":6,"code":"3","descriptor":"Detailed and accurate description of the theory, including its key claims and implications."}]},{"trait":"AO3 - Evaluation of the research evidence supporting and challenging the theory","maxMarks":6,"bands":[{"min":0,"max":0,"code":"0","descriptor":"No relevant evaluation."},{"min":1,"max":2,"code":"1","descriptor":"Evaluation fragmentary, generic or inaccurate; little use of research evidence."},{"min":3,"max":4,"code":"2","descriptor":"Some relevant evaluation using research evidence, but limited in depth or balance."},{"min":5,"max":6,"code":"3","descriptor":"Effective, well-balanced evaluation using both supporting and challenging research evidence, explicitly linked to the theory."}]}]},"answer":"AO1 - Bowlby's theory of maternal deprivation: the value of monotropy (attachment to one primary caregiver) means that prolonged separation from that caregiver (or failure to form an attachment) during the critical period (first ~2.5 years, extending to ~5 years for deleterious effects) has serious and permanent consequences for emotional, social and intellectual development - affectionless psychopathy (lack of guilt/empathy, leading to delinquency), delinquency, and developmental retardation (low IQ). Separation only becomes damaging if the child experiences prolonged separation/deprivation rather than brief separation (distress at separation is normal and not itself harmful). AO3 - Supporting evidence: Bowlby's 44 thieves study - 44 thieves compared with matched non-delinquent controls; 14 of the 44 thieves were affectionless psychopaths, and 12 of these had experienced prolonged early separation from their mothers, versus almost none in the control group, supporting the link between maternal deprivation and later maladjustment. Challenging evidence: Goldfarb - children institutionalised for longer periods showed poorer social and cognitive outcomes, but this confounds institutionalisation generally with maternal deprivation specifically. Rutter's ERA/Romanian orphan research shows that children who experienced severe early deprivation but were adopted before ~6 months largely recovered, challenging the idea of a strict critical period and permanent damage; effects appear related to duration and later care rather than the mother specifically. Lewis's partial replication of the 44 thieves study found that prolonged separation was associated with later problems but not with affectionless psychopathy or criminality specifically, and the association was not as strong as Bowlby claimed. Methodological criticisms: Bowlby's 44 thieves study relied on retrospective interviews (recall bias, social desirability), the researcher (Bowlby) knew which participants were thieves (researcher bias), and the design was correlational - deprivation may be a correlate rather than cause of delinquency; the sample was biased (clinic-referred boys). The theory has been criticised for conflating deprivation (loss of an attachment) with privation (never forming one), and for assuming the mother is the unique/essential caregiver - Rutter showed that children can form attachments with multiple caregivers and that it is disruption of attachment rather than absence of the mother per se that matters. Overall, the theory was historically influential (shaping hospital visiting arrangements, childcare policy) but the evidence suggests its claims were overstated: damage is not inevitable or permanent, and the critical period is better understood as a sensitive period.","acceptableAlternatives":["AO1: any accurate account of monotropy, critical/sensitive period, prolonged separation vs brief separation, affectionless psychopathy, delinquency, developmental retardation/low IQ","AO3 supporting evidence: Bowlby's 44 thieves study (14 affectionless psychopaths among thieves, most with prolonged separation), Goldfarb's institutionalisation findings, or other valid supporting research","AO3 challenging evidence: Lewis's partial replication, Rutter's ERA/Romanian orphan findings, criticism of critical period as too rigid, methodological criticisms of 44 thieves (retrospective data, researcher bias, correlational design, biased sample), conflation of deprivation with privation, assumption that mother is unique caregiver","Evaluation may be presented as separate supporting/challenging sections or integrated; either structure is acceptable","Concluding judgements may vary (e.g. theory historically influential but overstated; evidence supports some link but not inevitability) - credit any reasonable, evidence-based conclusion"],"commonMistakes":["Confusing maternal deprivation theory with Bowlby's monotropy/evolutionary attachment theory (internal working model, critical period for attachment formation)","Describing the Strange Situation or attachment types instead of maternal deprivation","Describing the 44 thieves study in detail without evaluating it","Presenting only supporting or only challenging evidence rather than both","Claiming the 44 thieves study was an experiment with manipulated variables rather than a correlational/case-control design","Confusing deprivation (loss of attachment figure) with privation (never forming an attachment)","Asserting that all children who experience separation become delinquent or affectionless psychopaths","Failing to link evaluation back to the theory itself"]}]}
